![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14158318/assets/ef5fe44009ea42457243052cff584a216ee94636d8e3c16ff9446e85b8eca551.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=1-5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{7\pi }{6},$ shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1-5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{(1-5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{1-10\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +25{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +25{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{1-10\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +25}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{26-10\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},$ shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{4+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{8}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{8}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =8(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\theta {e}^{\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi \,?$
questions.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\theta {e}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=(1+\theta ){e}^{\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(\theta {e}^{\theta })}^{2}+{((1+\theta ){e}^{\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{\theta }^{2}{e}^{2\theta }+(1+\theta )^{2}{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{e}^{2\theta }({\theta }^{2}+1+2\theta +{\theta }^{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{\theta }\sqrt{2{\theta }^{2}+2\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={cos}^{3}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2},$ shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={cos}^{3}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}){cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}).
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\sqrt{{({cos}^{3}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}))}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}){cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}))}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\sqrt{{cos}^{6}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})+{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}){cos}^{4}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\sqrt{{cos}^{4}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})[{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})+{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})]}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\sqrt{{cos}^{4}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}[1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\theta }{3})]\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[\theta +\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\theta }{3})]}_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
